[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal employer-employee matched datasets (e.g., LEHD) with firm-level union density measures and state-level minimum wage changes — Allows direct estimation of how firm-level union density moderates the relationship between industry-level concentration and individual earnings gains from minimum wage increases, addressing both levels of analysis.

[PATH:empirical] Difference-in-differences or event-study analyses of minimum wage hikes across industries with varying union density, using public-use CPS or SIPP data merged with industry concentration indices — Provides quasi-experimental variation to test whether unionized firms show different pass-through of minimum wage increases to net earnings compared to non-union firms, conditional on concentration.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of wage bargaining and monopsony (e.g., Manning 2003, Card & Krueger 1995) extended to incorporate union density as a moderating factor — Develops predictions about when and why union density might amplify or dampen the effect of employer concentration on minimum wage pass-through, guiding empirical specification and interpretation.

qualifier.temporal: post-2000, with focus on periods of minimum wage increases

[PATH:empirical] LinkedIn or administrative employer-employee matched panel data (e.g., LEHD) from a state with a large, sudden minimum wage increase and high union density (e.g., California or New York), combined with firm-level collective bargaining agreement records — This would allow direct estimation of how firm-level bargaining power (proxied by union contract coverage) moderates the gap between industry-level and individual-level estimates of employer concentration's effect on net earnings gains. Comparing difference-in-differences results across bargaining vs. non-bargaining firms within the same industry can isolate the attenuating effect.

[PATH:theoretical] Formal model of wage bargaining with oligopsony and minimum wage shocks (e.g., extension of Manning (2003) or Bhaskar & To (1999)) that incorporates firm-level collective bargaining agreements — Such a model can derive predictions about when and why firm-level bargaining power should reduce the divergence between industry-level and individual-level concentration effects. It would clarify the causal mechanisms and boundary conditions (e.g., large, sudden minimum wage increases) underlying the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on minimum wage effects that report both industry-level and individual-level concentration estimates, stratified by union density and collective bargaining coverage — A systematic review can assess whether the hypothesized pattern holds across multiple contexts (e.g., different countries, time periods, and minimum wage change sizes). It would provide statistical power to detect the moderating role of bargaining power and identify potential publication biases or confounding factors.
